summary:
The Wealden iron industry in south-eastern England used local ironstone, charcoal from coppiced woodland, and, from the late medieval period, water-powered furnaces and forges. Roman ironmaking was extensive: about 113 bloomery sites are known, with production estimated at 750 tons annually before falling after 250 AD. Smelting evidence disappears after Roman rule until the ninth century.

A blast-furnace process arrived at Buxted around 1490, and nearly 180 furnace or forge sites operated in the Weald between the 15th and 18th centuries. The industry peaked in the late 16th century, producing more than 9,000 tons of iron a year in the 1590s. It supplied London and became a major cannon producer, especially after 1650.

Wealden bar iron lost ground to Midland and imported Swedish iron. Cannon production continued until the Seven Years’ War, but price competition from coke-fired Scottish works and the lack of accessible coal led to the industry’s decline. Ashburnham forge was the last to close.
unsupportedClaims: The charcoal used by Wealden ironmakers came from coppiced woodland; the points say only that coppicing could provide a sustainable wood supply.
Wealden bar iron definitively lost ground to Midland and imported Swedish iron; the points describe the Midland explanation as possible and the inability to compete with Swedish imports as apparent.
Cannon production continued until the Seven Years’ War; the source says it remained a major activity until the end of the war.
